column1: # The Krate App Benchmark corpus.
# This measures a different thing from evidence/reliability/corpus.txt. That
# one asks "did authoring succeed" -- did something build and run. This one
# asks "is the result usable" -- would a person who asked for this app get an
# app that does the thing, survives being resized, answers a click, and stays
# open. A great many apps pass the first bar and fail the second, and the
# second is the one a real person feels.
# FORMAT: tab-separated, four fields.
#   id      Stable identity. NEVER reuse, reorder, or renumber. Append only.
#           A results file from any date is keyed by this and must stay
#           comparable to every other one.
#   tier    easy | medium | hard | refuse
#           easy    a single screen of static-ish state, no layout maths
#           medium  real state, several interacting parts, or persistence
#           hard    known to sit on or past a runtime limit we have not shipped
#           refuse  Krate genuinely cannot serve this; the pass is a fast,
#                   honest refusal, and building something plausible is a FAIL
#   request The words a person would actually type. Handed to `krate create`
#           verbatim, nothing prepended.
#   asserts Semicolon-separated observable properties. This is the answer to
#           "does what was asked" and the whole reason this file is a TSV and
#           not a list of sentences. See the contract below.
# THE ASSERTION CONTRACT
# Every assert is a claim about ONE line the app prints on stdout during its
# self-exercise run (`krate run <app> -- quick`). The harness does not read
# pixels and does not need a human after the first judgement.
# Assert grammar, all machine-evaluable:
#   key>=N        the app printed "key:V" and V, read as a number, is >= N
#   key<=N        same, <=
#   key==V        the app printed "key:V" exactly
#   key!=V        the app printed "key:V" and it is not V
#   key~text      the app printed "key:V" and V contains "text"
#   key?          the app printed a "key:" line at all, any value
# Why stdout and not a screenshot: a locked reference screenshot fails on every
# font, scale, and theme change and would have to be re-judged constantly, so
# it would rot into a rubber stamp within a month. A pixel diff also cannot
# tell "the counter went up" from "the counter is painted". Stdout state is the
# thing the request was actually about, it survives cosmetic change, and the
# convention already exists: 27 of the 34 apps in apps/ ship a `quick` path
# that drives themselves and prints their state. This benchmark makes that
# convention a requirement instead of a habit.
# The one-time human judgement: a person reads the request and writes the
# asserts. That judgement is then LOCKED in this file and re-run forever
# without a human. If an assert is wrong it gets fixed with a note in
# evidence/benchmark/RESULTS.md saying what changed and why, never silently.
# The asserts are the ONLY thing gate 3 checks. An earlier draft also demanded
# every app print `ready:1` and `quick:done`. That was dropped, deliberately:
# nothing in the authoring pack teaches those keys, so every app would have
# failed them and the score would have measured an invention of this harness
# instead of the product. A bar the product was never told to meet is not a
# measurement. "Stays open" is evidenced behaviourally instead -- the app exited
# cleanly and painted a frame.
# The assert VALUES must be bare: `total:57.23`, not `total:$57.23`. Apps do not
# reliably do this today (K-013 -- the pack says only "print something"), and
# that is a real, reportable failure rather than something to paper over here.
# CHANGE LOG. Every edit to a locked assert is recorded here.
# 2026-08-05, before the first run. Rows 14, 30, 33, 34 asserted `saved==1`,
# `roundtrip==1`, `tail==1`, `measured==1`. Checking against the 17 shipped
# bundles showed real apps write `saved:yes`, not `saved:1`. Those four asserts
# were therefore testing a naming convention rather than a capability, and an
# app that genuinely saved would have failed on spelling. Relaxed to `!=no`,
# which tests the thing the request is about. Nothing was relaxed because a run
# failed it -- this was caught before the run.
# HONESTY RULE. Do not delete or soften a row because we fail it. The hard tier
# exists because it is currently mostly red, and a benchmark that only holds
# what we pass is an advert. Rows may be added; a row may only be REMOVED if it
# turns out to be ambiguous or unjudgeable, and the removal is recorded.
# --- easy: one screen, little layout maths (1-12) ---

column1: # --- hard: sits on or past a limit we have not shipped (31-38) ---
# These are here to be failed today, and each one names the board entry that
# explains it. 31-33 need scrolling: K-001, no scroll event exists in the WIT,
# and K-004, no clip rect, so a scrolling list would draw over its own header.
# 34-35 need text measurement: K-002, every app fabricates a width constant.
# 36-38 are canvas apps that must survive a resize: K-003, canvas apps hard-code
# layout so hit-boxes stay put while the canvas stretches.

# Scored inverted. `krate create` must exit non-zero with a refusal that names
# the limit, and must NOT produce a .krate. Building something plausible here
# is the worst failure in the benchmark, because the person cannot tell.
